Open research instrument · v0.2

Twenty tests passed.
The bug was still there.

Two patches to the same ledger library print identical test output. Only one of them works. An agent that reads the report cannot tell them apart. An agent that runs a separate check can.

Witness asks what happens when many AI agents share that report. When their peers agree, do they stop checking for themselves?

Follow the argument ↓ Open the simulation

01 · The question

One report can sound like many.

Give that report to a team of agents. Each round, every agent decides how to spend a small, fixed budget: listen to peers, or pay to check the world directly.

  1. 1

    The report

    A few agents see “20 passed.” It is one observation, from one source, and it might be wrong.

    1 source
  2. 2

    The echoes

    Peers relay it. Six agents now agree, but every copy traces back to the same report. Agreement grew; evidence did not.

    still 1 source
  3. 3

    The check

    One agent spends its whole turn running the probe. The result arrives later, but it is a new observation that can overturn the consensus.

    new evidence

The tradeoff, in effort units

Every agent gets 4 units per round. Reading one peer message costs 1. Requesting a check costs all 4, and the result arrives after a delay. Both choices use the same budget.

Option 1 · listen
4 peer messages
or
Option 2 · verify
1 check, delayed

The hypothesis

Agreement may crowd out checking.

If agreement makes agents confident, they may spend less of their budget on checks. Fewer checks mean fewer new observations that could challenge the agreement. That loop would let a wrong report persist even though the truth was always one check away.

Status: plausible, not yet observed. The loop could be weak, absent, or even helpful when reports are true. Witness exists to measure it, not to assume it.

02 · The model

Test the idea in a model you can inspect.

A swarm of simulated agents passes the ledger claim around under three ways of weighing evidence. Every rule is written down, and every run can be replayed.

Authored rules, not LLM behavior. This model shows what follows from stated assumptions. It does not measure how real agents act. Read the rules ↗

    03 · Real models

    What a real language model did.

    Eight instances of one model, eight rounds, the same report and budget rules. Each agent saw only its own evidence and chose to check, relay, or abstain. These are its recorded decisions.

    Requested a checkRelayed an assessmentAbstainedMalformed outputStated support for the claim

    Rows are agents, columns are rounds. ● marks agents holding the original report; ◆ marks a delivered probe result. Select a cell to read the decision.

    Why this does not yet test the loop

    • The budget never forced a choice. One check plus seven relays used 11 of the 24 available units, so agents could check and still talk.
    • The check was free of doubt. Every agent could reach a definitive probe, and most requested it in round one, before any peers had spoken.
    • Agreement was not varied. The next experiment holds evidence and budget fixed and randomizes how many peers endorse the report.

    One model, one seed, one case family. No agent was ever mistaken, so these runs could not show the harmful loop. Full pilot report and failures ↗

    04 · Research program

    From instrument to finding.

    Each hypothesis states how it would be shown false. A null result counts: if reliable checking makes the loop disappear, that is worth knowing.

    H1

    Acquisition feedback

    Holding evidence fixed, more peer agreement lowers the chance an agent requests a check.

    False if checking stays flat or rises across controlled, held-out exposures.

    Next experiment
    H2

    Opportunity-cost harm

    Under a fixed budget, the lost checking raises error. Correlation between agreement and error is not enough.

    Test: replay matched runs on an externally fixed checking schedule.

    Proposed
    H3

    Ancestry helps

    Showing that endorsements share one source weakens the effect, rather than only improving static aggregation.

    Caution: the authored model above shows source tracking can also backfire.

    Proposed
    H4

    Reserved checking

    Keeping a small checking reserve cuts error on false reports at an acceptable cost on true ones.

    Fails if it spends effort without improving the accuracy-cost frontier.

    Proposed
    1. Stage 0

      Infrastructure

      Grounded fixtures, the inspectable model, a bounded decision harness with cost controls, and a first real-model pilot.

      Built
    2. Stage 1

      Local response

      Freeze an agent's state; randomize endorsing peers, independent sources, and whether shared ancestry is visible. Measure check probability across 24+ case families.

      Next
    3. Stage 2

      Close the loop

      16 to 64 agents, three model families, matched budgets. Compare agent-chosen checking with fixed and reserved schedules.

      Proposed
    4. Stage 3

      Fit and predict

      Fit transition rules from Stages 1 and 2, then test on held-out cases and graphs. Only then simulate at scale, labeled as extrapolation.

      Proposed

    Closest prior work, and the gap Witness targets

    Closest baselineEpistemic Sybil ResistanceBara · 2026

    Many reports need not mean many sources. Witness asks how that shapes the decision to check.

     Collective dynamicsPhysics of AgentsEl et al. · 2026

    Consensus regimes across AI communities are established. Evidence acquisition is the added variable.

     Verification delayDelayed Verification Destabilizes Multi-Agent LLM BeliefItkin · 2026

    Grounded answering removed its oscillation, a boundary condition for this project.

     Costly checkingLie Rarely, Lie BigAnand & Pappas · 2026

    Verification budgets under insider misinformation. Witness studies ordinary agreement, not adversaries.

     Social influenceToo Polite to DisagreeSIGDIAL 2026

    Peer sycophancy shifts outcomes. Witness measures checking behavior without assuming its cause.

     Scale is not noveltyAgentSocietyPiao et al. · 2025

    Already simulates 10,000+ agents. The browser's scale is engineering, not a finding.
